Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) scales outcome
supervision through executable validation
\citep{shao2024deepseekmath,guo2025deepseekr1}. Yet a conventional verifier
records only correctness: repeated copies and different successful outputs
receive the same scalar reward. A policy can therefore become more accurate as
its support over verified output modes contracts
\citep{liu2025understanding,cui2025entropy,dang2025diversity}. This limitation
weakens repeated sampling, best-of-$K$, and verifier-guided selection: once one
output dominates training, additional samples reproduce the familiar rather
than extend the set available to a selector
\citep{brown2024monkeys,snell2024testtime,cobbe2021training,lightman2023lets}.
Figure~\ref{fig:story} exhibits this failure on one prompt;
Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-precheck} shows it is systematic. Eight passes of
unmodified Dr.GRPO or GRPO remove $99\%$ and $98\%$ of the base model's
verified breadth beyond its first correct mode at Qwen2.5-0.5B, and
$42$--$72\%$ of it at the two larger scales.
In an idealized model, our analysis shows that additional parameters can
preserve more sampled alternatives at matched accuracy when they strengthen
updates shared across correct outputs
(Appendix~\ref{app:theory-size}, Theorem~\ref{thm:shared-correctness});
size alone provides no guarantee.

\noindent\textbf{Verifiable learning and output support.}
Repeated sampling and verifier-guided selection depend on proposal support
\citep{brown2024monkeys,snell2024testtime}, yet RLHF, fine-tuning, and RLVR can
narrow that support
\citep{kirk2024understanding,dang2025diversity,cui2025entropy,yue2025rlvrlimit}.

\citep{farquhar2024detecting}. \mb{} instead lets accepting execution define
the equivalence relation, yielding an exact behavioral key.
